items.stem: Define the term 'expert system'.
items.answer: A computer system that imitates the decision-making of a human expert in a particular field, using stored knowledge and rules.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A computer system that imitates the decision-making of a human expert in a particular field, using stored knowledge and rules. [2]

items.stem: Describe how the components of an expert system work together to give advice.
items.answer: The user interface asks questions and collects answers; the inference engine applies rules from the rules base to these answers and the facts in the knowledge base; it reaches a conclusion, which the interface displays with an explanation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 4. [4]

items.stem: Explain why an expert system cannot completely replace a human expert.
items.answer: It only knows the rules and facts it has been given, cannot use common sense or deal with unusual cases, and has no empathy; its knowledge must be kept up to date.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limited to programmed knowledge; 1 mark unusual cases/judgement/empathy. [2]

items.stem: Delta Water Utility in Muscat is developing an expert system to help staff give advice to customers. Explain why an explanation system is useful.
items.answer: Shows reasoning so users trust/check advice; helps training.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 2. [2]

items.stem: TransGlobal Logistics in Toronto is developing an expert system to help staff give advice to customers. (a) Describe the role of the inference engine. (b) Describe the role of the user interface.
items.answer: (a) Applies rules to facts and user input to reach conclusions (forward/backward chaining). (b) Asks questions, accepts answers and displays conclusions/explanations.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark per point, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Nadia is explaining to trainees at FreshFarm Foods in Bangkok how an expert system works. Discuss whether FreshFarm Foods should rely on an expert system rather than human specialists.
items.answer: Points for: consistent advice; available 24 hours; cheaper per query; stores knowledge of retiring experts. Points against / limitations: lacks common sense and empathy; only as good as its rules; expensive to build and maintain; legal responsibility for wrong advice. Conclusion: expert systems are best used to support, not replace, human specialists.

items.stem: Define the term 'forward chaining'.
items.answer: Reasoning that starts from the known facts and applies rules whose conditions are met to derive new facts, until a conclusion is reached (data-driven).

items.stem:
An expert system for plant health advice has these rules:
R1: IF leaves are yellow AND soil is wet THEN plant is overwatered
R2: IF plant is overwatered THEN water less often
R3: IF leaves have white powder THEN mildew infection
R4: IF mildew infection AND weather is humid THEN spray with fungicide
R5: IF leaves are yellow AND soil is dry THEN plant is underwatered
R6: IF plant is underwatered THEN water more often
The known facts are: soil is dry; leaves have white powder; weather is humid. Using forward chaining (checking rules in order and repeating until no rule can fire), state which rules fire, in order, and the new facts derived.
items.answer: Rules fired: R3, R4; new facts: mildew infection; spray with fungicide
items.markingKey: Rules fired: R3, R4; new facts: mildew infection; spray with fungicide (1 mark per rule fired in correct order, 1 mark for conclusions, max 3). [3]

items.stem:
An expert system for loan advice has these rules:
R1: IF income is regular AND credit history is good THEN low risk applicant
R2: IF low risk applicant AND deposit is at least 10% THEN approve the loan
R3: IF credit history is poor THEN high risk applicant
R4: IF high risk applicant THEN refer to a manager
R5: IF income is irregular AND credit history is good THEN medium risk applicant
R6: IF medium risk applicant THEN offer a smaller loan
The known facts are: income is regular; credit history is good; deposit is at least 10%. Using forward chaining (checking rules in order and repeating until no rule can fire), state which rules fire, in order, and the new facts derived.
items.answer: Rules fired: R1, R2; new facts: low risk applicant; approve the loan
items.markingKey: Rules fired: R1, R2; new facts: low risk applicant; approve the loan (1 mark per rule fired in correct order, 1 mark for conclusions, max 3). [3]

items.stem:
An expert system for car fault diagnosis has these rules:
R1: IF engine will not start AND lights are dim THEN battery is flat
R2: IF battery is flat THEN recharge or replace the battery
R3: IF engine will not start AND starter clicks THEN starter motor fault
R4: IF starter motor fault THEN replace the starter motor
R5: IF engine overheats AND coolant level low THEN coolant leak
R6: IF coolant leak THEN repair the radiator hose
The known facts are: engine overheats; coolant level low; engine will not start. Using forward chaining (checking rules in order and repeating until no rule can fire), state which rules fire, in order, and the new facts derived. Using backward chaining instead, explain whether the goal "repair the radiator hose" can be proved from the known facts.
items.answer: Rules fired: R5, R6; new facts: coolant leak; repair the radiator hose; backward chaining: "repair the radiator hose" can be proved
items.markingKey: Rules fired: R5, R6; new facts: coolant leak; repair the radiator hose (1 mark per rule fired in correct order, 1 mark for conclusions, max 3).; backward chaining result (proved) with reasoning through the rules [2]. [5]

items.stem:
An expert system for car fault diagnosis has these rules:
R1: IF engine will not start AND lights are dim THEN battery is flat
R2: IF battery is flat THEN recharge or replace the battery
R3: IF engine will not start AND starter clicks THEN starter motor fault
R4: IF starter motor fault THEN replace the starter motor
R5: IF engine overheats AND coolant level low THEN coolant leak
R6: IF coolant leak THEN repair the radiator hose
The known facts are: engine will not start; starter clicks. Using forward chaining (checking rules in order and repeating until no rule can fire), state which rules fire, in order, and the new facts derived.
items.answer: Rules fired: R3, R4; new facts: starter motor fault; replace the starter motor
items.markingKey: Rules fired: R3, R4; new facts: starter motor fault; replace the starter motor (1 mark per rule fired in correct order, 1 mark for conclusions, max 3). [3]

items.stem: Coral Bay Aquarium in Toronto is building an expert system for car fault diagnosis. An expert says: "If engine will not start and starter clicks, then starter motor fault." (a) Write this knowledge as a rule for the rules base. (b) Explain how the inference engine would use this rule in forward chaining. (c) Describe how the knowledge engineer would check that the rule is correct.
items.answer: (a) IF engine will not start AND starter clicks THEN starter motor fault (b) When all conditions are in the known facts, the rule fires and "starter motor fault" is added as a new fact, which may allow further rules to fire. (c) Discuss with experts, test with real cases and compare the system's conclusions with experts' decisions.

items.stem: Ethan is a knowledge engineer working for Summit Engineering in Singapore. Evaluate the difficulties Summit Engineering may face in creating an expert system.
items.answer: Points for: experts may struggle to explain intuitive knowledge; experts may disagree; time and cost; knowledge changes. Points against / limitations: once built, the system captures expertise permanently and gives consistent advice; benefits may outweigh costs. Conclusion: the system is worthwhile if experts are committed and it is maintained.
